cards.answer: Manual review of the 10,000-image test set found about 8 to 10 genuinely sensitive images, or about 1% of the corpus. At that low prevalence, even a highly accurate model produces more false positives than true positives. The semantic method achieved 16.5% precision on flagged items, reflecting the ambiguity of archival content. Human Remains and Violence/Graphic Content were the most reliably detected categories, as descriptions map cleanly to unambiguous terms. Native American Imagery and Historical Racialized Performance were harder, as descriptions often lacked explicit cultural context cues.

cards.answer: I built a topic clustering pipeline for the file archive using TF-IDF on document summaries and KMeans with elbow-method K selection to find the archive’s thematic structure without manual labeling. I assigned top 20 keywords per cluster to LLaMA, which generated human-readable one-sentence topic titles. A second hierarchical pass created subtopics with their own titles. cards.answer: For Skyrule, I tested seven OCR and vision models against professional transcriptions, measuring character error, word accuracy, speed, and how often each invented or repeated text. cards.answer: I built an OCR pipeline for Skyrule, my personal project, that sorts every page by type first, then uses multiple models to read each page. Their disagreement becomes a per-page quality score, routing uncertain pages to stronger readers or a review queue. Combining several readers was more accurate than the best single model. Every page keeps a record of its source, which models read it, how much they agreed and which reading was kept. In production, it read 6,910 pages from 45 books in about 7.6 GPU-hours.

cards.answer: I built a career transition matrix using employees' job title sequences to identify the most likely next roles and simulate career paths with a Markov chain. By walking transitions stochastically through simulate_career_path() and summarizing outcomes with simulate_many_paths(), I mapped where roles like Academic Advisors might end up after four moves. links.label: Procurement intelligence: The Unit Normalization Problem

cards.answer: I built a pack-size normalization system to uncover true per-unit pricing in procurement data, using the qsu field (quantity sold as), which is populated for 99.9% of rows (6,068,599 of 6,068,888). By dividing catalog price by qsu, I identified 23% of rows (1,395,917) needing normalization. For example, a $317 case of 500 versus a $14 pack of 50 looked like a big saving, but normalization reduced the estimated savings from $317,583 to $161,564, removing $156,019 (49.1%) of pack-size inflation.

cards.answer: I built a three-tier procurement pipeline. Tier 1 is an exact match on manufacturer and part number, a dict lookup under 2ms with no AI, which found 42,052 matched pairs. Tier 2 used FAISS with bge-small-en-v1.5 over 5.19M vectors, filtering 6M rows to about 50 candidates at cosine similarity of at least 0.85. cards.answer: I built a procurement intelligence system that processed 6,068,888 catalog rows and identified 42,052 exact-matched product pairs across four distributors. The median unit-price spread was 20.7%, and 37,535 additional matched pairs show price gaps but lack volume data. This estimate is a defensible floor, not a ceiling, waiting on quantities from the remaining distributors to refine the total.

cards.answer: I built a pipeline to sync research proposals between Kuali and the analytics warehouse, bridging two Oracle databases with no dblink. cards.answer: I built a text-extraction pipeline using PyMuPDF to handle research proposals, including a magic-byte validator that catches DOCX files misnamed as PDFs. Invalid files are tagged with reason codes and sent to a rejection bucket instead of halting the batch. Text is filtered against a pre-cached vocabulary of about 500K words, combining NLTK, WordNet lemmas, and wordfreq thresholds. cards.answer: I built a 26-field taxonomy for the NSF HERDS classification, using a curated keyword list with no overlaps and eight reassignments per keyword. I embedded each proposal using SentenceTransformer and multiplied against a pre-computed taxonomy matrix to classify in one operation. I blended semantic and keyword scores at 0.75 / 0.25, with a 0.12 threshold for final labels. This method outperformed either signal alone on the validation set.

cards.answer: I built a predictive model for UIC student continuation using H2O Random Forest, selecting features through variable importance, SHAP values, and partial dependence plots. Time-in-program factors like completed terms and academic years emerged as the most predictive for both graduate and undergraduate students. Early top variables, GRAD_STATUS_DESC and AH_ACAD_YEAR_CD_LIST, were removed due to leakage risk. Continuation probability rose sharply up to 8 terms, plateauing around 0.91 after 10, showing early-term students carry the highest dropout risk. cards.answer: I trained separate Tree Ensemble models for each semester (Summer, Spring, and Fall) to capture term-specific dropout patterns at UIC. Alpha and beta parameters were tuned from 0.05 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05 using an 80/20 train-validation split, selecting the pair with the lowest validation RMSE. The best model was refit on all data to produce a 10-period forecast, with uncertainty given as point forecast plus or minus validation MAE.

cards.answer: I designed a controlled vLLM evaluation using 50 bills, each 4,500 to 4,972 Mistral tokens, to test three 7B-8B AWQ models: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct. Setup included vLLM 0.6.6, AWQ-Marlin, --max-model-len 8192, prefix caching, and a 5-call warmup. Cross-repeat variance stayed under 0.5% throughput, 1.5% p99 latency, and 0.3pp quality.

cards.answer: I designed Experiment 3 by scoring 60 cells on Accuracy, Specificity and Completeness using a 0 to 2 rubric. Claude Opus 4.8 evaluated it in two passes, high effort then max effort, and agreed on 60 out of 60 with no revisions. This showed parse-OK reliably ranks models in the same order as substantive scoring. But Experiment 3.5 found parse-OK fails as a within-model proxy: smaller chunks scored higher on substance in every informative pair. The issue was off-section drift. Larger chunks led models to confidently fill fields from adjacent sections.

cards.answer: I designed a rubric with three dimensions (Accuracy, Specificity and Completeness) each scored 0 to 2. Accuracy judged faithfulness to the chunk, from wrong (0) to faithful (2). Specificity measured from generic boilerplate (0) to naming the actual mechanism (2). Completeness tracked from surface phrases (0) to substantive points captured (2). The per-cell average was (Accuracy + Specificity + Completeness) divided by 3.

cards.answer: I reviewed how context-window size affects extraction fidelity in vLLM, testing 500, 1200, and 3000-token configurations. The 1200-token setup stayed on-chunk most reliably, while 3000-token pulled in unrelated bill sections and lost key headlines. On six self-contained single-amendment bills, all three models converged near 2.0. But on multi-section bills, Mistral collapsed while Llama held. This showed the effect is a property of the configurations, model, and chunk size together, not the models alone.

cards.answer: I ran Phase 2 of quality validation to check if parse-OK ranks chunk sizes correctly within each model. I compared informative pairs and found that smaller chunks scored at least as well as larger ones, with no agreement between parse-OK and quality peaks for Llama, Qwen, or Mistral. Larger chunks caused off-section drift, with models confidently answering about the wrong part of a bill. Across five within-model pairs, there were three reversals, one tie, and one agreement. This did not change the production recommendation: Llama still leads by 20+ percentage points.

cards.answer: I analyzed failure patterns in Qwen and Mistral using vLLM, finding that off-section drift is the dominant issue. Models confidently answer about the wrong section at larger chunk sizes. At chunk_size=3000, Qwen returns parse_status=OK with all 11 fields as None, a hidden failure. The quality gap is concentrated in Completeness, while Specificity remains stable. Both models drift to the same wrong section on the same HB4820 chunk, showing a shared mechanism across model families.

cards.title: The root cause of agent failure

cards.answer: Most failures come from one assumption: the model is smart enough to handle everything. It's not. Not yet. The systems that work handle preprocessing upfront, clean and structure data, provide schema-level context, design retrieval carefully, and use prompts that preserve context and coherence. cards.title: Agent, workflow or RPA?
questions: how do you choose between a simple model and a complex one?

when would you not use ai at all?
cards.answer: Agent territory: ambiguous decisions, logical reasoning, evolving inputs. The example I use is scraping trending topics in news. You can't hard-code what's trending, it changes constantly, and the model has to look at generalities and pick top themes. That's genuine agent work. Workflow automation: static process, consistent algorithm, consistent input and output. Same shape data coming in, same shape data going out. Don't use an agent for that. RPA: the simplest stuff, standard ETL, standard in and standard out. Old-school data science methods handle this perfectly. You don't need an AI agent. Rule of thumb: if the task requires the system to interpret something that isn't clearly defined, it's an agent. If it doesn't, it isn't, and forcing AI into it just adds complexity and cost.

cards.title: Are AI agents a real paradigm shift?
questions: what do you think ai will do to the world over the next 10 to 20 years?
are ai agents a paradigm shift
are agents just automation with better ux
what is different about ai agents
will agents change how we work
cards.answer: Yes. I don't think agents are just an evolution of automation and APIs with better UX. They're a real shift in how work gets done. The part that's fundamentally different is ambiguity. Traditional pipelines follow deterministic logic, rule-based, conditional, predictable in. Agents operate where the decision isn't something you can hard-code. Where the model has to make a judgment call on fuzzy inputs. That's both the power and the risk. You're handing off the ambiguity to the AI, and whatever it decides is what happens next. If you think your role is safe, it probably isn't. Within the next 6 to 12 months, tasks, not whole jobs, but tasks, are going to start getting stripped out of roles at an accelerating pace. Whether that's a problem depends on your job. If it's mostly repetitive, yeah, be concerned. If it involves real decision-making, stakeholder work, strategy, and business impact, you're likely fine, but your job will evolve.

cards.title: The non-negotiable in an agent system
questions: how do you design a system that fails safely and tells you when it fails?
what is non-negotiable when designing an agent system
how do you stop ai drift
how do you anchor llm outputs to truth
how do you detect model drift
old school and new school validation

cards.answer: There has to be a way to anchor outputs back to truth. AI systems drift. The more they build on prior outputs, the worse it gets. So you need a base truth layer, validated data, known-good outputs, plus a way to detect drift and cross-check results. Some tolerance for variation is fine. Unlimited deviation isn't. My concrete example: in my legislation work, I have the Llama model generating category labels (new-school) and I also have an old-school clustering model generating categories from keywords (old-school). Both produce taxonomies. If one says Higher Education and the other says K-12 for the same bill, that's a flag. I can isolate the mismatches, inspect them, and figure out whether the model drifted or the data is weird. Hybrid validation like that is essential.

Then you double-check the data, double-check the calculations. AI-generated deterministic code you can read and trust beats an agent black-boxing it every single time.

cards.answer: Everyone says 'AI augments humans' but most of the time that's vague or not really true. Both are happening simultaneously. The difference is what kind of work and how much oversight exists. Real augmentation: AI helps you move faster, you still own the outcome. You review, validate, correct, make the final call. AI accelerates, humans stay responsible for correctness. Where humans must stay in control right now: hiring, firing, legal outcomes, financial decisions, anything that directly affects someone's life. Those need multiple layers of review: the person who built the system approves how it works, stakeholders own the decisions, and someone audits continuously. Without that, it's not augmentation, it's uncontrolled automation in a trench coat.

cards.answer: When I was extracting 10+ structured features from legislation text, I originally thought asking each question separately would make parsing cleaner and more predictable. Turns out that's wrong. Bundling the questions in the same prompt gave better results because the model uses its earlier answers as context for later ones. If it already established 'this impacts higher education' and 'this affects students,' then when I later ask 'does this impact the university,' it answers yes coherently, and when I ask 'rate the impact as slight/moderate/very impactful,' it uses everything it just figured out. Context builds within the prompt. Isolating tasks too much loses coherence and reasoning continuity. Prompt engineering isn't just asking questions, it's designing the context the model reasons inside.

cards.answer: In my legislation work, some bills were massive outliers, over 100,000 tokens, roughly 100x the size of a normal bill. Only about 5% of the data, but they added enormous noise. They were amendment-heavy bills, the same content updated over and over with every small change. Most of it added no context. What actually mattered was the latest changes, maybe the last thousand tokens. If you feed those directly into an AI system without preprocessing, it chunks them inefficiently, wastes compute, takes hours to process the worst-quality subset, and pollutes everything downstream. The fix wasn't an AI fix. It was a preprocessing fix. Detect the outliers, summarize them as 'amendment type, last changes attached,' and move on. cards.answer: People box ROI into time saved, cost reduced, revenue generated. That's incomplete. One of AI's most underrated capabilities is extracting insight that was previously inaccessible. What are the things you don't know? What are you losing because you didn't know them? That's the cost of not knowing, and it's where AI really earns its place. My legislation work is the clearest example. Being aware of what's being proposed before it passes lets you prevent losses and find opportunities. In HR, detecting where roles are shrinking or growing ahead of time is strategic intelligence. Not time. Not cost. Better decisions, better strategy, better plans.

cards.title: The model needs to know what the data means
questions: how do you evaluate an llm or a rag system? what metrics do you trust?
does an llm need a data dictionary
why does metadata matter for ai
how do you give a model schema context
how does a model understand my tables
help a model understand our database tables
cards.answer: Even if the data is technically correct, if the model doesn't understand what the fields represent, it'll produce confident garbage. Poorly named columns, encoded values with no explanation, missing metadata, no documentation, all of it breaks the system quietly. You need a context layer: a data dictionary or 'data cookbook,' metadata descriptions, schema explanations embedded into prompts. It needs to know what each field represents, how fields relate, and what the data is actually capturing. Without that you're asking it to interpret something it doesn't understand, and it'll happily make something up.

cards.answer: Some of these risks are still unknown. There's always potential for things getting hacked into. Maintenance overhead. Infrastructure complexity. Older or smaller models have logic and reasoning that's nowhere near the frontier. But it's a trade-off. Sometimes you don't need the frontier. It's about what you need and what the trade-offs are. Don't self-host because it sounds cooler. Self-host because the use case requires the control.

questions: how do you decide whether an ai system is good enough to ship? how do you know it works?

cards.answer: In the AI era, things look convincingly right even when they're wrong. Code generation is fast. Analysis is fast. But so much of it is wrong in subtle ways. The real job now is validation, combing through line by line, column by column, asking where the data came from, whether it makes sense. If I'm getting 100% accuracy on a model, something is wrong. If everything is falling into place too easily, something is wrong. The job of a data scientist now is to slow it down.
